previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of morbid obesity, chronic lymphedema, recurrent cellulitis, diastolic heart failure, and prior DVT/PE was admitted for worsening right lower extremity pain, erythema, and swelling with fever and leukocytosis. She was started on IV vancomycin and clindamycin for suspected cellulitis. After initial improvement, her infection worsened following transition to oral clindamycin, prompting re-initiation of IV vancomycin. Infectious disease recommended continuing IV therapy with aggressive edema management. Her swelling, attributed to lymphedema and heart failure, was managed with IV furosemide and bumetanide, with transition to oral diuretics. A low INR of 1.5 led to a thrombolytic dose via PICC and continued warfarin, though INR remained subtherapeutic at discharge (1.7). A positive C. difficile PCR without diarrhea was not treated. Pain was managed with oxycodone, morphine, and IV dilaudid, with recommendations for outpatient opioid weaning. She developed a non-infectious blister on the left calf. By discharge, infection had improved, and she was transitioned to oral doxycycline and cephalexin. She was discharged home with services, Narcan, and follow-up instructions for antibiotics, diuretics, INR monitoring, and PICC line evaluation.

Other epilepsy, not intractable, without status epilepticus

of contrast.  Bilateral lower extremity varicosities are noted.

LOWER CHEST: Minimal atelectasis is noted in the lung bases. There is no
pleural or pericardial effusion.

ABDOMEN:

HEPATOBILIARY: The liver demonstrates homogenous attenuation throughout. There
is no evidence of focal lesions. There is no evidence of intrahepatic or

without stones or gallbladder wall thickening.

PANCREAS: The pancreas has normal attenuation throughout, without evidence of
focal lesions or pancreatic ductal dilatation. There is no peripancreatic
stranding.

SPLEEN: The spleen shows normal size and attenuation throughout, without
evidence of focal lesions.

ADRENALS: The right adrenal gland is unremarkable.  Within the left adrenal
gland is in unchanged 2.6 x 3.4 cm heterogeneously enhancing lesion which
measures 9 Hounsfield units on noncontrast consistent with adrenal adenoma. 
(02:22; 3: 51).

URINARY: Bilateral simple renal cysts noted.  The kidneys otherwise are of
normal and symmetric size with normal nephrogram. There is no evidence of
stones, focal renal lesions, or hydronephrosis. There are no urothelial
lesions in the kidneys or ureters. There is no perinephric abnormality.

GASTROINTESTINAL: Small bowel loops demonstrate normal caliber, wall thickness
and enhancement throughout. Colon and rectum are within normal limits.  Again
seen is a moderate-sized duodenal diverticulum measuring 3.6 x 2.7 cm along
the second portion the duodenum (3:94).  Appendix is not visualized.  There is
no evidence of mesenteric lymphadenopathy.

RETROPERITONEUM: There is no evidence of retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.

PELVIS: Urinary bladder is decompressed.  There is no evidence of pelvic or
inguinal lymphadenopathy.  There is no free fluid in the pelvis.

REPRODUCTIVE ORGANS: The visualized reproductive organs are unremarkable.

BONES: There is no evidence of worrisome osseous lesions or acute fracture.

SOFT TISSUES: The abdominal and pelvic wall is within normal limits.

LOWER EXTREMITY: No acute fracture.  Surgical changes from prior right ACL
repair is noted.  No focal lytic or blastic lesions worrisome for malignancy. 
No acute fracture.  There is severe symmetric bilateral subcutaneous edema
with skin thickening involving the lower extremities extending from the knees
through the ankles with relative sparing of the feet.

IMPRESSION:


1. Severe symmetric bilateral subcutaneous edema with skin thickening
involving the lower extremities with patent venous vasculature up to the
popliteal veins.  Findings likely related to lymphedema.  Assessment of the
peroneal and posterior tibial veins is limited due to timing of contrast
study.
2. 3.4 cm left adrenal adenoma.
3. Moderate duodenal diverticulum.

TECHNIQUE:   OPERATORS: Dr. ___ Radiologist and Dr. ___
___, Interventional Radiology fellow performed the procedure. Dr.
___ supervised the trainee during any key components of the
procedure where applicable and reviewed and agrees with the findings as
reported below.
ANESTHESIA: 1% lidocaine was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues
overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS:
CONTRAST: 10 ml of Optiray contrast
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  2.5, 25 mGy


PROCEDURE:
1. Right basilic venogram.
2. Single lumen PICC placement via brachial access.
PROCEDURE DETAILS:
The right arm was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  The PICC
was noted to be significantly pulled back.  A guidewire was introduced through
the existing PICC and advanced into the right atrium.  The existing PICC was
removed over the wire.  A 4.5 ___ peel-away sheath was advanced over the
wire into the basilic vein however was then able to be Foley advanced.  The
PICC was advanced over the wire through the sheath into the vein that was
unable to be advanced past the axillary vein.  The PICC was removed over the
wire and contrast was injected through the peel-away sheath.  The vessel lumen
is noted to be stenotic to the level of the brachiocephalic vein.  The
peel-away sheath was kept in place to maintain access.

Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, the brachial vein was punctured
under direct ultrasound guidance using a micropuncture set. Permanent
ultrasound images were obtained before and after intravenous access, which
confirmed vein patency. A peel-away sheath was then placed over a guidewire.
The guidewire was then advanced into the superior vena cava using fluoroscopic
guidance. A PIC line was then placed through the peel-away sheath with its tip
positioned in the distal SVC under fluoroscopic guidance. Position of the
catheter was confirmed by a fluoroscopic spot film of the chest. The peel-away
sheath and guidewire were then removed. The catheter was secured to the skin,
flushed, and a sterile dressing applied.

The basilic vein peel-away sheath was then removed and manual pressure was
held until hemostasis was achieved.

The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  Long segment stenosis of the basilic vein.
2.  The accessed brachial vein was patent and compressible.
3.  Brachialvein approach single lumen PICC with tip in the distal SVC.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a right 47 cm brachial approach single lumen PowerPICC
with tip in the distal SVC.  The line is ready to use.
